en: In the Gautama Dharma Sūtra:
"The Veda is the root of dharma" (1). "And the tradition and conduct of those who know it" (2).
A transgression of the Dharma and great recklessness are observed among the great, but not so in matters of perceptible reality due to the weakness of inferior beings. (3)
When there is a conflict between two rules of equal strength, there is an option. ||4||
The initiation (*upanayana*) of a Brāhmaṇa takes place in the eighth year; in the ninth or fifth year, it is optional (*kāmya*). The count of years begins from conception (*garbha*).
That is the second birth. (8) For he is the teacher because of that. (9) And because of the recitation of the Vedas. (10)
For the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, [the initiation] occurs in the eleventh and twelfth years respectively. ||11||
The *sāvitrī* [initiation] does not lapse for a Brāhmaṇa until the sixteenth year; for a Rājanya, until the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya, until two years beyond that.

The girdles are made of muñja grass, of bowstring hemp (maurvī), and of wool, respectively. (15) The skins are those of the black antelope, the spotted deer, and the goat, respectively. (16) The garments for all are made of hemp, of linen, of bark-cloth, and of kutapa wool. (17) And [the garment] may also be made of unprocessed cotton. (18) Some say that even a saffron-colored (kāṣāya) garment is permitted. (19) A garment made of tree-bark is for the Brāhmaṇa. (20) Madder-red and yellow are for the other two [castes].

(21) The staffs of the Brāhmaṇa are made of Bilva or Palāśa wood. (22) For the remaining [castes], they are made of Aśvattha or Pīlu wood. (23) Or, for all, they may be made of any wood suitable for sacrifice. (24) They should be undamaged, curved like a sacrificial post, and possessed of their bark. (25)
Their sizes are equal to the crown of the head, the forehead, and the tip of the nose, respectively. ||26||
And those with shaven heads, matted hair, topknots, and tangled locks. ||27||
If one has something in hand while being impure from food remnants, one should set it down and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana). ||28||

The purification of substances consists of wiping, heating, scraping, and washing for objects made of metal, clay, wood, and woven cloth. (29) Objects made of stone, gems, conch-shells, and mother-of-pearl are purified like those made of metal. (30) Bone and earth are purified like wood. (31) And for the ground, sowing [with seeds] is also a means of purification. (32) Ropes, mats of split bamboo, and skins are purified like cloth. (33) Alternatively, there shall be discarding of those that are excessively defiled. (34)

One should begin the act of purification facing either the east or the north. (35) Seated in a clean place, having placed his right arm between his knees, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, and having washed his hands up to the wrists, he should remain silent and sip water three or four times so that it touches his heart; he should wipe his mouth twice, sprinkle water on his feet, touch the cavities of the head, and apply water to the crown of his head. (36) He must do this again after sleeping, eating, and sneezing. (37)

Regarding food stuck between the teeth, [the purification is] as with the teeth, except when touched by the tongue. (38) Some say it is until the food falls out. (39) When they have fallen out, one should know that the purification is like that for saliva; one becomes pure simply by swallowing them. (40)
Drops that do not fall upon the body do not make one impure with leavings. ||41||

Purification for that which is smeared with impurities consists in the removal of the stain and odor; first, this is done with water and earth [43]. And [this purification is required] in cases of contact with urine, feces, semen, exudations, or food [44].
And where the sacred tradition (Āmnāya) would enjoin [it].

Having grasped the teacher’s left hand with his own, excluding the thumb, he should address the teacher, saying: “Recite, sir! (46). Thereupon, he should fix his gaze and mind [on the teacher] (47). He should touch his vital breaths with *darbha* grass (48). There are three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), each consisting of fifteen *mātrās* (49). And he should sit on a seat whose blades point eastward (50). The five *vyāhṛtis*, preceded by *oṃ* and ending with *satya*, [are to be recited] (51).

52. The clasping of the teacher’s feet takes place in the morning. 53. And [it occurs] at the beginning and at the end of the recitation of the Veda. 54. Having been permitted, the pupil should sit down to the south, facing east, or facing north. 55. The Sāvitrī verse and the recitation [of the Veda follow]. 56. At the beginning of the acquisition of the Veda, [the Sāvitrī is recited] first. 57. The syllable *oṃ* is used even elsewhere.

Furthermore, in the case of entering [a village] between [the times for study], there is a return to the initiation ceremony (upasadana). (58) In the case of [the death of] a dog, a mongoose, a snake, a frog, or a cat, there is fasting for three days and staying away from home. (59) For other [animals], there are breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and the consumption of clarified butter (ghṛtaprāśana). (60) And likewise in the case of studying near a cremation ground; and likewise in the case of studying near a cremation ground. (61)
Thus ends the first chapter in the Gautama Dharma Sūtra.

Before the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) may act, speak, and eat according to his desire; he may void urine and feces wherever it happens. (1) No rule for ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) applies to him, except for wiping, washing, and sprinkling. (2) There is no impurity resulting from contact with him. (3) However, one should not employ him in the offering of the fire-oblation (*agnihotra*) or the presentation of the food-offering (*bali*). (4) One should not cause him to recite the *brahma* (the Veda), except for the pouring of the *svadhā* libation. (5)

The rules [of student life] begin with the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). (6) Student celibacy (*brahmacarya*) has been described. (7) [These include] tending the sacred fire, gathering fuel, begging for alms, speaking the truth, and performing ablutions. (8) Some [teachers] say they begin with the *godāna* ceremony. (9) And there is the practice of performing the twilight devotions outside [the village]. (10)
He should stand during the first watch [of the night] and sit during the last, remaining silent as long as the stars are visible, or until the appearance of light; he must not look at the sun.

One should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, sleeping during the day, collyrium, ointments, vehicles, shoes, umbrellas, lust, anger, greed, delusion, singing, playing musical instruments, bathing, brushing the teeth, exhilaration, dancing, singing, slander, and fear. (13) In the presence of the teacher, one should avoid covering the neck, sitting with knees bound by a cloth (*avasakthika*), leaning against a support, and stretching out the feet. (14) One should avoid spitting, laughing, yawning, and cracking the knuckles. (15) One should avoid looking at or touching women, even when there is a suspicion of sexual intercourse. (16) One should avoid gambling, associating with the low-born, taking what is not given, and violence. (17) One should avoid uttering the names of the teacher, his son, his wife, or those who have been initiated. (18) One should avoid harsh words. (19) A Brahmin should avoid liquor at all times. (20)
He should sleep on a low bed or seat, rise before others, and go to rest after them; he should restrain his speech, his arms, and his stomach.

One should mention the name and lineage of the teacher with respect. (23) One should do the same when honoring or when [the teacher] is superior. (24) One should respond [to a command] after leaving one's bed, seat, or standing place. (25) One should go toward [the teacher] even if not seen, upon being called. (26) Upon seeing the teacher, one should rise from a lower position, a seat, or while sitting cross-legged, and likewise when using the wind [for bodily functions]. (27) When the teacher is departing, one should follow him after having informed him of one's duties and announced them. (28) One should study when summoned. (29) One should be intent on what is pleasant and beneficial [to the teacher]. (30)

The same applies to their wives and sons. (31) One should not eat the remnants of their food, nor bathe, adorn, wash the feet of, massage, or clasp the feet of [these relatives]. (32) Upon returning from a journey abroad, one should clasp the feet of the wives of one's gurus. (33) Some say this does not apply to young women, provided one has attained the age of marriageable adulthood. (34)

One should go for alms among all social classes, excluding those who have been formally accused of a crime and those who have fallen from their caste. (35) The word *bhavat* (sir/madam) should be employed at the beginning, middle, and end [of the request], according to the order of the classes. (36) When it is not possible [to obtain food] from these, one may seek it elsewhere from teachers, paternal relatives, and gurus. (37) Among these, one should avoid each preceding one in preference for the succeeding one. (38)

Having offered [the food] to his teacher, he should eat when permitted; 39. in the teacher’s absence, [he should eat] having offered it to the teacher’s wife, his son, a fellow-student, or a virtuous person. 40. Restraining his speech, eating until satisfied, and not being greedy, he should keep water close at hand. 41.

The correction of a student shall be carried out without corporal punishment (AV 1.34.42). In case of incapacity [to restrain him], it may be done with a thin rope or a split bamboo cane (AV 1.34.43). One who strikes [a student] with anything else must be punished by the king (AV 1.34.44).
One should practice the life of a student (brahmacarya) for twelve years regarding a single Veda; or for twelve years for each [Veda]; or until [the Veda] has been mastered.
At the conclusion of his studies, the teacher should be invited with a gift; or, having performed the ritual, the student may bathe once he has received permission.
The teacher is the best among gurus. Some say it is the mother; some say it is the mother.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Gautama Dharmasūtra.

Some state that there is a classification of these stages of life: the student, the householder, the mendicant, and the forest-dweller. Among them, the householder is the source, because the others do not produce offspring.

In this regard, it has been said concerning the religious student (brahmacārin): [Sūtra 4] Dependence upon the teacher lasts until the end [of life]. [Sūtra 5] He should recite his prayers with what remains from the duties for the teacher. [Sūtra 6] In the absence of the teacher, his conduct [of dependence] is toward the teacher’s offspring. [Sūtra 7] In their absence, it is toward an elder fellow-student or toward the sacred fire. [Sūtra 8] One who conducts himself thus and has conquered his senses attains the world of Brahman. [Sūtra 9]
And this is not in contradiction with those that follow. ||10||

A monk is one who has no accumulation [of possessions]. (11) He is one whose vital energy flows upward (*ūrdhvaretas*). (12) During the rainy season, he should be firm in his conduct. (13) Seeking alms, he should enter the village. (14) He should wander at the last part of the day, not returning [until the next morning]. (15) He should abstain from eating when the [time for] begging has ceased. (16) He should be restrained in speech, sight, and action. (17) He may wear a garment only for the purpose of covering his private parts. (18) Some say it should be worn after washing it once it has become soiled. (19) He should not take any part of plants or trees that has not been detached [from its source]. (20) He should not stay in a village for a second night except during the [proper] season. (21) He may be either shaven-headed or wear a top-knot. (22) He should avoid the destruction of seeds. (23) He should be impartial toward all beings, whether in their injury or their favor. (24) He should refrain from initiating any [injurious] activity. (25)

The Vaikhānasa dwells in the forest, subsisting on roots and fruits, and is devoted to austerity. (26) Having established the *śrāmaṇaka* fire, (27) he eats food that is not from a village. (28) He worships the gods, the ancestors, humans, spirits, and sages. (29) He is a host to all guests, except for those who are prohibited. (30) He may even consume the meat of a deer. (31) He should not step upon land ploughed by a plow. (32) And he should not enter a village. (33) He has matted hair and wears rags or skins. (34) He should not eat more than once a year. (35)
But the teachers maintain that there is only one stage of life, because the householder's life is directly enjoined. 36.
Thus ends the third chapter in the Gautama Dharmasūtra.

A householder should marry a wife who is suitable, not previously married to another, and younger than himself. (1) Marriage is with those who do not share the same *pravara* lineages. (2) [This applies] up to the seventh generation on the father’s side among paternal kinsmen. (3) And [up to the seventh generation] on the side of the progenitor (*bījī*). (4) [It applies] up to the fifth generation on the mother’s side among maternal kinsmen. (5)

In the *brāhma* form, he should give [the daughter] adorned and clothed to one who is endowed with learning, good conduct, kinship, and virtue. (6) In the *prājāpatya* form, the mantra for union is: "May you practice dharma together. (7) In the *ārṣa* form, he should give a pair of cattle to the groom of the maiden. (8) The *daiva* form consists of giving her as a gift to the officiating priest within the sacrificial enclosure after she has been adorned. (9) The *gāndharva* form is the union of two who desire each other by their own accord. (10) The *āsura* form is the purchase of women through wealth. (11) The *rākṣasa* form results from abduction by force. (12) The *paiśāca* form results from approaching her while she is unconscious. (13)
The first four [categories] are lawful; some say there are six.

Those born from women of the same caste who are one, two, or three degrees lower in the natural order are known as Savarṇa, Ambaṣṭha, Ugra, Niṣāda, Dauṣyanta, and Pāraśava. Those born in the inverse order are Sūta, Māgadha, Āyogava, Kṣattṛ, Vaidehaka, and Caṇḍāla.

From the Brāhmaṇa woman were born sons from the [other] castes in order: the Brāhmaṇa, Sūta, Māgadha, and Caṇḍāla. From those same [Kṣatriyas] were born by the Kṣatriya woman the Mūrdhāvasikta, Kṣatriya, Dhīvara, and Pulkasa. From those same [Vaiśyas] were born by the Vaiśya woman the Bhṛjjakaṇṭha, Māhiṣya, Vaiśya, and Vaideha. From those same [Śūdras] were born the Pāraśava, Yavana, and Karaṇa; some say these are Śūdras.

The transition to another caste occurs through the seventh [generation] by means of either advancement or decline; according to the teachers, it occurs in the fifth generation; and this also applies to those born in other creations.

But those born in the reverse order are devoid of dharma. (25) And [the son] born of a Śūdra woman [is likewise]. (26) From a Śūdra, [a son] born of a woman not of equal status has the livelihood of an outcast. (27) The last [of these] is the most sinful. (28)

Virtuous sons purify [their lineage]. (29) [They purify] three generations on the father’s side through the *ārṣa* rite. (30) Ten [generations] on the father’s side through the *daiva* rite. (31) And ten [generations] on the mother’s side through the *prājāpatya* rite. (32) A son born of the *brāhma* rite purifies ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself. (33)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Gautama Dharmasūtra.
He should approach his wife during her season; or he may do so at all times, except when it is forbidden.

He should worship the gods, ancestors, humans, spirits, and sages. (3) He should engage in the daily private recitation of the Veda. (4) He should also offer water to the ancestors. (5) Other rites may be performed according to his inclination. (6) The sacred fire is either that of the wife or that of the inheritance. (7) In that fire, the domestic rites are performed. (8)
The sacrifices to the gods, the ancestors, and humans, as well as the private recitation of scripture and the offering of oblations. ||9||
The oblations are offered to Agni in Agni, to Dhanvantari, to the Viśvedevas, to Prajāpati, and to Sviṣṭakṛt. 10.

And to the deities of the quarters, each according to their respective direction; ||11|| to the Maruts at the doors; ||12|| having entered, to the deities of the house; ||13|| to Brahmā in the center; ||14|| to the Waters by the water-jar; ||15|| saying "To Ākāśa," in the intermediate space; ||16|| and to the night-wanderers in the evening. ||17||

The giving of alms after reciting a benediction is unprecedented (and thus highly meritorious). (18) And the same applies to righteous gifts given to those who bestow them. (19) The fruits [of such giving] are equal, double, a thousandfold, or infinite, depending on whether the recipient is a non-Brahmin, a Brahmin, a learned scholar (*śrotriya*), or one who has mastered the Vedas (*vedapāraga*). (20) Outside the sacrificial altar (*bahirvedi*), there should be a distribution of goods to those seeking for the sake of their teacher, for a wedding, for medicine, for the sake of livelihood, those whose means are exhausted, those about to perform a sacrifice, those engaged in Vedic study, those traveling on a journey, and those dedicated to universal charity (*vaiśvajita*). (21) To those begging, cooked food should be given; to others, other types of food. (22)

Even after having given a promise, one should not give if it is connected with unrighteousness. (23) The words of those who are angry, exultant, terrified, afflicted, greedy, childish, aged, dull-witted, intoxicated, or insane are untruths that do not constitute a sin. (24)

One should feed first the guests, the young, the sick, pregnant women, newly married women, and the elderly; those who are inferior should be fed last. However, the act of cooking must be announced to the teacher, one's father, and friends.

The honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) is offered upon the arrival of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), teachers (*ācārya*), fathers-in-law, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles; [this is repeated] again after one year. It is also offered before a sacrifice or a wedding. And [it is offered] to a king who is a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*). To one who is not a *śrotriya*, however, only a seat and water are provided. But for a *śrotriya*, one should provide water for the feet (*pādya*), the guest-offering (*arghya*), and various kinds of food. Or rather, it should always be specially prepared. The gift of food is placed in the middle [of the meal] for one who is of good conduct but not a *śrotriya*. In the opposite case, however, [only] grass, water, and ground are given. Finally, a welcome is offered to everyone.

And one should also avoid excessive honor [from them]. (37) Lying down, sitting, attending upon, following after, and serving are equal toward those who are equal and toward those who are superior. (38) Even to a small degree, [these acts] should be performed for one who is inferior. (39)

A guest from a different village is one who stays for only a single night and waits upon the sun while remaining under a tree. (40) One should inquire after his welfare, well-being, and health. (41) For a Śūdra, this [inquiry] is the final [duty]. (42) A non-Brāhmaṇa is not a guest for a Brāhmaṇa, unless he has arrived at a sacrifice. (43) However, the meal for a Kṣatriya is after the Brāhmaṇas. (44) Others [should be fed] together with the servants for the sake of compassion—for the sake of compassion. (45)
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Gautamīya Dharmasūtra. ||5||

1. One should perform the clasping of the feet every day when meeting [elders] in a group. 2. But one should do so after approaching them upon returning from a journey. 3. This applies to one's mother, father, their relatives, ancestors, teachers of knowledge, and the teachers of those teachers. 4. When several elders are assembled together, one should perform the salutation toward the most senior among them. 5. In a gathering of those who know the proper form of address, one should announce one's own name, saying, "I am so-and-so," and then perform the salutation. 6. Some say there is no fixed rule regarding the salutation when a man and a woman are present together. 7. One need not perform the salutation for women who are not one's mother, paternal aunt, wife, or sister, even if they have returned from a journey. 8. Nor should one perform the clasping of the feet for the wives of one's brothers or for one's mother-in-law. 9. However, one must rise to greet officiating priests, fathers-in-law, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles, even if they are younger; they are not to be saluted by bowing down. 10. Likewise, any other person who is senior—whether he be a village headman over eighty years old or even a Śūdra—is to be treated as an equal to one's own children. 11. Even a younger Ārya (member of the higher castes) is to be treated as an equal by a Śūdra.

And one should avoid using his [the teacher’s] name. (12) A king is not to be addressed by name; he is to be called "messenger. (13) One born on the same day is to be addressed as "friend," "sir," or "honorable one. (14) A fellow citizen who is ten years older is to be addressed as "sir. (15) One who possesses five arts is to be addressed as "sir. (16) A learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) who is three years older is to be addressed as "sir. (17) One who performs the duties of a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya and is devoid of learning is to be addressed as "sir. (18) And one who has been consecrated for a sacrifice is to be addressed as "sir" until the purchase of the Soma. (19)

Wealth, kinship, occupation, birth, learning, and age are grounds for respect, provided they are more powerful than the others. (20) But sacred knowledge (*śruta*) is weightier than all of these. (21) For dharma has its root in that. (22) And because it is so stated in the Veda. (23)

The way must be yielded to a wheel-turning monarch, one who stands at the tenth stage, a person worthy of favor, a bride, a student who has completed his studies, and a king. But the king must yield the way specifically to a learned Brahmin (śrotriya).
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Gautama Dharma Sūtra.

In times of distress, it is permissible for a Brāhmaṇa to acquire knowledge from one who is not a Brāhmaṇa. (1) Following him and serving him are required. (2) Once the study is completed, the Brāhmaṇa becomes his teacher. (3)

Sacrificing for others, teaching, and receiving gifts are [the means of livelihood] for all [twice-born classes]. (4) Each preceding one is more venerable than the following. (5) In the absence of that, the occupation of a Kṣatriya [is permitted]. (6) In the absence of that, the occupation of a Vaiśya [is permitted]. (7)

His merchandise consists of [the following]: (8) perfumes, liquids, prepared foods, sesame seeds, hemp, linen, and skins; (9) dyed and bleached garments; (10) milk and its derivatives; (11) roots, fruits, flowers, herbs, honey, meat, grass, water, and unwholesome items; (12) and animals, provided they are not associated with slaughter. (13) Furthermore, he must always avoid human beings, oxen, young girls, and barren cows. (14) According to some teachers, land, rice, barley, goats, sheep, horses, bulls, milch-cows, and draft-oxen are also forbidden. (15) However, there is a restriction: (16) liquids may be exchanged for liquids, (17) and animals for animals. (18) But this does not apply to salt and prepared foods, (19) nor to sesame seeds. (20) When raw grain is exchanged for cooked food, it is permissible provided the quantities are equal. (21)

In every way, however, one who is unable [to subsist by his own duty] may live by the occupation of a Śūdra, provided it is not that of a Śūdra [in the strict sense]. Some say this is permitted even when there is a danger to life. But there is a restriction regarding the mixing of castes and the consumption of forbidden food. When there is a danger to life, even a Brāhmaṇa may take up arms; a Rājanya may perform the work of a Vaiśya; and a Vaiśya may likewise perform the work of a Vaiśya.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Gautama Dharma Sūtra.

In this world, two uphold their vows: the king and the learned Brāhmaṇa. Upon them depends the livelihood of the fourfold human race—those with internal consciousness, as well as those that move, fall, and crawl. Their duty consists of procreation, protection, and the prevention of intermixture.

He is one who has heard much (bahuśruta). (4) He knows the world, the Vedas, and the Vedāṅgas. (5) He is skilled in the dialogues (vākovākya), the Itihāsas, and the Purāṇas. (6) He depends on them and lives according to them. (7) He is consecrated by the forty purificatory rites (saṃskāra). (8) He is devoted to the three duties (karman), or to the six. (9–10) He is well-trained in the rules of customary conduct (sāmayācārika). (11)
One should be avoided by the king for six reasons: [one who is] not to be killed, not to be imprisoned, not to be punished with fines, not to be banished, not to be censured, and not to be avoided.

Conception, the rite for a male child, parting the hair, birth-rites, naming, the first feeding of solid food, the tonsure, and initiation; ||14|| the four Vedic vows; ||15|| the ceremonial bath, union with a wife, and the performance of the five sacrifices to the gods, ancestors, humans, spirits, and Brahman; ||16|| and of these [sacrifices], ||17|| the Aṣṭakā, the Pārvaṇa, the Śrāddha, the Śrāvaṇī, the Āgrahāyaṇī, the Caitrī, and the Āśvayujī—these are the seven forms of cooked-sacrifice (pākayajña). ||18|| The establishment of the sacred fires, the Agnihotra, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Āgrayaṇa, the Cāturmāsya, the Nirūḍhapaśubandha, and the Sautrāmaṇī—these are the seven forms of oblation-sacrifice (haviryajña). ||19|| The Agniṣṭoma, the Atirātra, the Ukthya, the Ṣoḍaśin, the Vājapeya, the Atirātra, and the Aptoryāma—these are the seven forms of Soma-sacrifice. ||20|| Thus, these are the forty sacraments (saṃskāras). ||21||
Now, there are eight personal virtues: compassion toward all living beings, patience, freedom from envy, purity, lack of exertion, auspiciousness, lack of miserliness, and lack of longing.

He who possesses these forty sacraments but does not possess the eight qualities of the self does not attain union with Brahman nor residence in the same world as Brahman. However, he who indeed possesses even a portion of the forty sacraments and also the eight qualities of the self, he attains union with Brahman and residence in the same world as Brahman—yes, he attains them.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Gautama Dharmasūtra.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rule and having taken a wife, he who practices the duties of a householder as they have been described should observe these following vows. ||1||

A Snātaka should always be pure, fragrant, and habituated to bathing. (2) If he possesses the means, he should not wear worn-out or dirty clothes. (3) He should not wear dyed, gaudy, or clothing previously worn by another. (4) Nor should he wear garlands or shoes [belonging to others]. (5) If he lacks the means, he may wear washed [clothing]. (6) He should not let his beard grow long without a specific reason. (7)

One should not hold fire and water simultaneously. (8) One should not drink from one's cupped hands. (9) One should not perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) while standing with water drawn up [in a vessel]. (10) Nor should one do so with water poured by a Śūdra, by an impure person, or with [the water] offered by only one hand. (11)
One should not cast away urine, feces, or impure substances while looking toward the wind, fire, Brahmins, the sun, water, deities, or cows. One should not extend one's feet toward these deities.

One should not remove urine or feces with leaves, clods of earth, or stones (14). One should not stand upon ashes, hair, husks, potsherds, or impure things (15). One should not converse with barbarians, the impure, or the unrighteous (16). Having conversed [with them], one should meditate in the mind upon those who perform meritorious deeds (17). Or, one should converse with a Brāhmaṇa (18).

One should call a non-cow "one fit to be a cow" (dhenubhavyā). One should call what is not auspicious "auspicious" (bhadra). One should call a skull "the mark of fortune" (bhagāla). One should call Indra’s bow "a jeweled bow" (maṇidhanus).
One should not point out to another a cow suckling her calf; nor should one drive her away.

Having engaged in sexual union, he should not delay in performing purification. (25) Nor should he recite his Vedic lessons while lying on that same bed. (26) Nor, having studied during the final watch of the night, should he go back to sleep again. (27) He should not take pleasure with a woman who is unwell. (28) Nor with one who is menstruating. (29) Nor should he embrace her. (30) Nor a maiden. (31)

He should avoid blowing on fire with his mouth, engaging in contentious speech, wearing external perfumes and garlands, scratching himself with his fingernails, eating together with his wife, looking at himself while applying collyrium, entering by a side door, washing his feet with his feet, eating while seated on a bench, crossing a river by swimming with his arms, climbing up or down a tree or a precipice, and exerting himself to the point of risking his life. (32) He should not board a boat whose safety is uncertain. (33) He should protect himself from all dangers whatsoever. (34)

One should not wander about during the day with one’s head covered; however, one may do so at night. (35–36) One should also do so when voiding urine or excrement. (37) One should not do so on the bare ground without having covered it [with grass or leaves]. (38) Nor should one do so from a doorway or a dwelling. (39) Nor should one do so in ashes, in cow-dung, in ploughed land, in the shade, on a path, or in a place desired by others. (40) During the day, one should perform both urination and defecation facing north. (41) And so too during the two twilights. (42) But at night, one should face south. (43)
One should avoid using a seat made of *pālāśa* wood, as well as sandals and a tooth-stick. (44) Furthermore, one should avoid eating, sitting, saluting, or prostrating while wearing shoes. (45)

One should not let the forenoon, midday, or afternoon pass fruitlessly; rather, one should devote them to dharma, artha, and kāma according to one's ability. Among these, however, one should make dharma the primary concern.

One should not look at another man’s wife while she is naked. (48) One should not drag a seat with one’s foot. (49) One should not engage in the restlessness of the genitals, stomach, hands, feet, speech, or eyes. (50) One should not, without cause, perform cutting, piercing, scratching, rubbing, or lashing. (51) One should not walk over a rope to which calves are tied. (52) One should not be a "family-to-family" beggar (one who begs from every house). (53) One should not go to a sacrifice unless invited. (54) However, one may go at will for the sake of seeing it. (55)

One should not eat food placed on one's lap. (56) One should not eat what has been brought by a female servant at night. (57) One should not eat items such as clarified butter from which the oil has been extracted, molasses, oil-cakes, or buttermilk, once their potency has been lost. (58) However, in the evening and in the morning, one should eat food that has been honored, without finding fault with it. (59)

One should never sleep naked at night, nor should one bathe naked. (60–61) One should practice that which those who are self-possessed, aged, well-disciplined, free from hypocrisy, greed, and delusion, and learned in the Vedas, declare. (62) For the sake of security and prosperity, one should seek refuge in the Lord; not anyone else, except for gods, teachers, and righteous persons. (63–64) One should strive to dwell in a residence where firewood, water, fodder, *kuśa* grass, and garlands are abundant, which is easy to exit, populated mostly by noble people, prosperous and free from laziness, and presided over by righteous men. (65) One should circumambulate clockwise sacred objects, auspicious signs, temples, crossroads, and the like. (66)

Or, as an alternative course in times of distress, he may observe that entire code of conduct mentally. (67) He should be devoted to truth and righteousness. (68) He should follow the conduct of the noble. (69) He should be a teacher of the disciplined. (70) He should be refined by purity. (71) He should be intent upon the sacred revelation. (72) He should always be non-violent, gentle, firm in action, and characterized by self-restraint and generosity. (73)
A Snātaka who conducts himself in this manner, seeking to liberate his parents and his ancestors and descendants from misfortunes, never falls from the worlds of Brahman; he never falls. 74.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Gautama Dharma Sūtra.
For the twice-born, [the duties are] study, sacrifice, and giving. ||1||

For a Brāhmaṇa, teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts are additional [means of livelihood]. (2) However, there is a restriction regarding the former [three]. (3) Teaching the Veda may be given to a teacher, a relative, a friend, a guru, one who provides wealth, or for the sake of learning, even when not restricted by the aforementioned rules. (4) Agriculture and trade are also permitted, provided they are not performed by oneself. (5) And money-lending is likewise permitted. (6)

The king’s primary duty is the protection of all living beings. (7) He must administer justice through appropriate punishment. (8) He should support Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas. (9) He should also support non-Brāhmaṇas who lack the means for a livelihood. (10) And he should support those who are exempt from taxes. (11) And he should support those who are engaged in religious studentship. (12)

And [the king] should provide assistance in victory; (13) especially in times of fear. (14) And he should practice [chariot warfare] with chariots and bows. (15) In battle, there should be a fixed formation and no retreat. (16) There is no fault in causing injury in combat. (17) Except in the case of those who are without horses, charioteers, or weapons; those with joined palms; those with disheveled hair; those with their backs turned; those who are seated; those on the ground; those mounted on trees; messengers; cows; Brahmins; and those who are proclaiming [their innocence]. (18) If another [caste], such as a Kṣatriya, should subsist by that [profession], he may live according to that occupation. (19) The victor shall take the booty acquired in battle. (20) But the mounts belong to the king. (21) And a special share (*uddhāra*) is granted when the victory is not achieved separately [by each unit]. (22) As for the rest, the king shall distribute it according to merit. (23)

The farmers shall pay a tenth, an eighth, or a sixth part of their produce as tribute to the king. (24) Some maintain that this applies to cattle and gold as well; [in that case], the share is one-fiftieth. (25) The toll on merchandise is one-twentieth. (26) For roots, fruits, flowers, medicinal herbs, honey, meat, grass, and firewood, the share is one-sixtieth. (27) This is because it is the duty of the state to protect these goods. (28) However, the king should be constantly vigilant regarding them. (29) His livelihood shall be from the surplus. (30)

Artisans shall perform one day’s work each month [for the state]. (31) By this, those who subsist by their own labor are explained. (32) So too are boatmen. (33) One should provide them with food. (34) Merchants shall deliver their merchandise at a price reduced according to the decrease in market value. (35)

Having found lost property that has no owner, they shall announce it to the king. (36) After having proclaimed it for one year, it must be guarded by the king. (37) After that period, the finder shall receive a fourth part, and the remainder belongs to the king. (38)

The owner [is established] in cases of inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure, and finding. (39) What is obtained by a Brāhmaṇa is his additional [share]. (40) What is won in battle belongs to a Kṣatriya. (41) What is earned through service belongs to a Vaiśya and a Śūdra. (42) The discovery of a treasure-trove is the property of the king. (43) It is not so in the case of a learned Brāhmaṇa. (44) Some say that even a non-Brāhmaṇa who reports it shall receive a sixth part. (45)

Having recovered property stolen by thieves, he shall restore it to its rightful place; or he may provide it from his own treasury. Property belonging to minors shall be protected until they reach legal majority or attain the age of discretion.
For a Vaiśya, agriculture, trade, animal husbandry, and moneylending are additional [duties]. 49.

The Śūdra is the fourth caste; he has a single birth. (50) For him also, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and purity [are required]. (51) Some say that for the purpose of ritual sipping (*ācamana*), there is only the washing of the hands and feet. (52) The performance of *śrāddha* rites; (53) the maintenance of dependents; (54) devotion to his own wife; (55) and service to those who rank above him. (56) He should seek his livelihood from them. (57) [He may accept] worn-out sandals, umbrellas, clothing, brooms, and so forth. (58) He may eat the remnants of their food. (59) And he may subsist by a craft. (60) Whichever Ārya he may rely upon, even if impoverished, he must be supported by him. (61) And the one above him [must support] him. (62) His accumulation of wealth should be for that purpose. (63) The *namaskāra* formula is prescribed as his mantra. (64)

"Some say that one should sacrifice for oneself with *pākayajña* offerings; moreover, all [members of the family] should attend upon each other in ascending order of seniority. When there is an interchange between an Ārya and a non-Ārya in the performance of a rite, the result is equal, it is equal."
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Gautama Dharmasūtra.

The king has authority over all, with the exception of the Brāhmaṇas. (1) He should be a doer of good and a speaker of what is right. (2) He should be thoroughly trained in the three Vedas and in Ānvīkṣikī (philosophy). (3) He should be pure, have his senses under control, and be endowed with virtuous associates and the means [of success]. (4) He should be impartial toward his subjects. (5) And he should act for their welfare. (6)

Others, besides the Brahmins, should sit below him as he sits above; they too should honor him. He shall protect the social classes (*varṇas*) and the stages of life (*āśramas*) according to the law. He shall establish those who have strayed back in their own duty (*svadharma*). For it is known that one becomes a sharer in the merit of dharma [by doing so].

And he should appoint as his domestic priest (purohita) a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with learning, noble lineage, eloquence, beauty, youth, and good character, who is of righteous conduct and ascetic. (12) Impelled by him, he should perform his ritual acts. (13) For it is known from sacred tradition that the Kṣatriya power, when impelled by the Brāhmaṇa, prospers and does not falter. (14) He should also pay heed to those things which those who contemplate divine portents and omens might proclaim. (15) For some maintain that even one's acquisition and preservation of property (yogakṣema) depends upon them. (16) He should perform in the domestic fire (śālāgni) rites connected with prosperity—such as those for pacification, auspicious days, well-being, longevity, and blessings—as well as those intended for causing enmity, subjugation, malevolent magic, and the ruin of enemies. (17) Other rites should be performed by officiating priests (ṛtvij) according to the prescribed rules. (18)

His legal practice consists of the Veda, the Dharmaśāstras, the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), the secondary Vedas (upavedas), and the Purāṇa. (19) The customs of regions, castes, and families that are not in conflict with the sacred traditions (āmnāyas) are authoritative. (20) Farmers, merchants, herdsmen, moneylenders, and artisans shall each abide by their own respective classes. (21) Having ascertained the facts from them according to their respective jurisdictions, he shall establish the legal decision. (22)

Reasoning is the means for attaining right knowledge. (23) Having inferred by means of it, one should lead [the student] to the truth according to the respective place. (24) In the case of disagreement, having brought [the matter] back from those who are elders among the knowers of the three Vedas, one should lead him to a final conclusion. (25) For in this way, his supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) comes to be. (26)

It is known that Brahman, when conjoined with Kṣatra, sustains the gods, the ancestors, and human beings. Punishment is called *daṇḍa* because of its power to subdue; therefore, one should subdue those who are unsubdued by means of it.

The social classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*), when established in their own duties, experience the fruit of their actions after death; then, by the remainder [of that karma], they obtain a birth distinguished by superior country, caste, family, form, lifespan, sacred learning, conduct, wealth, happiness, and intelligence. (29) Those who act otherwise, being contrary [to this path], perish. (30) Their protection is ensured by the instruction of the teacher and by punishment. (31) Therefore, the king and the teacher are beyond reproach; they are beyond reproach. (32)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Gautama Dharmasūtra.

A Śūdra who, having insulted or assaulted twice-born men with verbal or physical violence, shall have that very limb by which he committed the offense cut off. (1) For violating an Āryan woman, there shall be the excision of his organ and the confiscation of his property. (2) If she was under protection, the punishment shall be execution. (3) Furthermore, for one who listens to the Veda while it is being recited, his ears shall be filled with molten tin or lac. (4) For repeating it, his tongue shall be cut out. (5) For memorizing it, his body shall be torn apart. (6) One who seeks equality with a superior in sitting, lying down, speech, or on the road shall be fined. (7)

A Kṣatriya shall pay one hundred [paṇas] for insulting a Brāhmaṇa; for assault, double that amount. A Vaiśya shall pay one hundred and fifty. But a Brāhmaṇa shall pay fifty for insulting a Kṣatriya, and half of that for insulting a Vaiśya. He shall pay nothing at all for insulting a Śūdra. The rules for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya insulting each other are the same as those for a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya.

The guilt of theft for a Śūdra is eightfold. 15. For the other castes, it increases twofold for each successive class. 16. When a learned man commits an offense, the punishment is more severe. 17. For taking fruits, green crops, grain, or vegetables, the fine is five kṛṣṇalas when the amount is small. 18.

If cattle are harmed [while grazing], the fault lies with the owner [of the field]. (19) But if they are accompanied by a herdsman, the fault lies with him. (20) On a path or in an unenclosed field, the fault lies with both the herdsman and the owner of the field. (21) For a cow, the fine is five *māṣas*. (22) For a camel or a donkey, it is six. (23) For a horse or a buffalo, it is ten. (24) For goats or sheep, it is two each. (25) In the case of total destruction [of the crop], the full value must be paid as compensation. (26)

If one fails to perform prescribed duties or engages in prohibited acts, one must always undergo the forfeiture of one's own property once the value of a piece of cloth has been exceeded. (27) For the sake of cows or fire, one may take grass and fuel, as well as flowers from creepers and trees, and fruits from plants that are not enclosed by a fence, as if they were one's own. (28)

Interest on a loan is lawful at the rate of five *māṣakas* per month for every twenty [units of principal]. (29) Some say it should not exceed one year’s interest. (30) When a loan remains outstanding for a long time, the amount of the principal may double. (31) Interest does not accrue on a pledge that has been used. (32) Nor does it accrue on a pledge when the debtor intends to repay but is prevented from doing so. (33) There is also interest calculated by the wheel (*cakravṛddhi*). (34) Furthermore, there are interest paid by bodily labor (*kāritā*), interest paid in kind (*kāyikā*), interest paid as a lump sum (*śikhā*), and the use of a pledge (*ādhibhoga*). (35) In the case of loans involving livestock, wool, fields, grain, or draft animals, the total interest shall not exceed five times the principal. (36)

The property of one who is not an idiot or a minor, if enjoyed by others for ten years in the presence of the owner, belongs to the possessor. (37) This does not apply in the case of a learned *śrotriya*, a renunciant, or a royal officer. (38) In the case of cattle, land, and women, mere enjoyment is not sufficient [to establish ownership]. (39)

Those who inherit the estate shall discharge the debt. (40) Surety-money, commercial profits, customs duties, fines for liquor, gambling, and judicial penalties shall not devolve upon the sons. (41) Treasure-troves, deposits, items borrowed for use, articles purchased on credit, and pledges shall not be lost to the heirs if they were all blameless and there was no fault on the part of the person in charge. (42)

A thief, with disheveled hair and carrying a club, shall go to the king proclaiming his deed; he is purified by either execution or release. By failing to execute him, the king becomes a partaker in the guilt.

There shall be no corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa. [The punishments are] deprivation of office, public proclamation of the offense, banishment, and branding. If he does not adopt a proper mode of life, he must perform penance.
A minister who acts with deliberate intent is equal to a thief; so too is a recipient [of gifts] when it is joined with unrighteousness.

The application of punishment follows from the knowledge of the persistence of the offender's personal capacity and fault; or rather, there may be acquittal based on the statement of a consensus among those learned in the Vedas—based on the statement of a consensus among those learned in the Vedas. (Sūtras 51–52)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Gautama Dharmasūtra.

When there is a disagreement, the determination of truth is based on witnesses. (1) There should be many who are blameless in their own duties, trustworthy to the kings, and free from partiality or malice toward either party. (2) Even Śūdras may serve as witnesses. (3) However, a Brāhmaṇa, if he is not bound by ties and has not been coerced, cannot be restrained from speaking against a non-Brāhmaṇa. (4)

Those who are not members [of the court] shall not speak unless questioned. (5) And they would be at fault if they fail to speak. (6) Heaven results from speaking the truth; in the opposite case, hell. (7) Even those who are not formally appointed as witnesses may speak. (8) There should be no insistence on causing pain [to others]. (9) And the same applies to what is spoken through negligence. (10) Fault lies with the witnesses, the assessors, the king, and the judge when there is injury to the administration of justice. (11) Some say that the act of making [the testimony] true is accomplished by an oath. (12) That [oath] should take place in the assembly of gods, kings, and Brahmins for those who are not Brahmins. (13)

In the case of lying regarding small livestock, a witness destroys ten [ancestors]. (14) Regarding cows, horses, humans, and land, he destroys ten times more [successively]. (15) Or rather, in the case of land, he destroys everything. (16) For the theft of land, there is hell. (17) It is the same as for land in the case of water. (18) And likewise when it concerns sexual intercourse. (19) It is like the case of small livestock in the case of honey and clarified butter. (20) It is like the case of a cow in the case of clothing, gold, grain, and the Veda. (21) In the case of vehicles, it is like the case of horses. (22) A witness who speaks falsely is to be reproached and punished. (23) There is no fault in speaking untruth if one's livelihood depends upon it. (24) But not if it is for the livelihood of a wicked person. (25)

The king, or a learned Brāhmaṇa acting as judge, shall preside over the court. (26) He shall address the judge. (27) In cases where the defendant fails to respond, he shall wait for one year. (28) In matters concerning cows, oxen, women, or offspring, he shall act with haste. (29) And likewise in urgent matters. (30)
Truthful speech is weightier than all other things; truthful speech, truthful speech! 31.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the Gautama Dharmasūtra.

The impurity on account of a death (śāva-āśauca) lasts for ten nights for the sapindas, except for those who are officiating priests, those consecrated for a sacrifice, and students of sacred knowledge. (1) For a Kṣatriya, it lasts for eleven nights. (2) For a Vaiśya, it lasts for twelve nights. (3) Some say it lasts for half a month. (4) For a Śūdra, it lasts for one month. (5) If another [impurity] should occur within that period, they shall be purified by the remainder of the first period. (6) If it occurs when only one night remains, they are purified after two nights. (7) If it occurs at dawn, they are purified after three nights. (8)

[The impurity lasts] immediately for those killed by cows or Brahmins (sūtra 9); also for those killed through the king's wrath (sūtra 10); and in battle (sūtra 11). And for those who desire it, [the impurity ends immediately] when they die by means of fasting, starvation, weapons, fire, poison, water, hanging, or falling [from a precipice] (sūtra 12).
The cessation of the offering of rice-balls occurs in the seventh or the fifth generation. ||13||
The same applies to birth [as a cause]. (14) That [birth] belongs to the mother and father. (15) Or it belongs to the mother alone. (16)
The nights equal in number to the months of gestation [are the period of impurity] upon the miscarriage of the fetus; or it is three days.

And having heard [of a death], for one beyond the tenth day, there is impurity for two days and nights (pakṣiṇī). [Impurity lasts] for three days in the case of a kinsman not of the same sapinda-lineage, a relative by birth, or a fellow student; for one day in the case of a fellow student of the Veda (sabrahmacārin); and likewise for a learned scholar (śrotriya) who has arrived [as a guest].

If one intentionally touches a corpse, there is impurity for ten nights; this has been stated regarding the touch of a Vaiśya or a Śūdra. Or [there is impurity] for as long as the flow of blood lasts, or for the two preceding [classes]. Or it is for three days. And the same applies in the case of the teacher, his son, a wife, a person for whom one officiates at a sacrifice, and a pupil.

If a person of lower caste should touch one of higher caste, or a person of higher caste should touch one of lower caste, in that case the period of impurity is declared to be the same as that prescribed for a corpse.

Upon touching an outcaste (patita), a Caṇḍāla, a woman who has recently given birth (sūtikā), a menstruating woman (udakyā), or a corpse, or upon touching someone who has touched them, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on. (30) And also upon following a corpse [to the cremation ground]. (31) And also upon [touching] a dog. (32) Some say that this applies whenever one is defiled by such contact. (33)

The offering of water is performed by the sapinda relatives for one who has grown matted hair; ||34|| and also for his wives. ||35|| Some say it is for those who have been given away in marriage. ||36||

All [the mourners] shall sleep on the ground, remain seated [on the floor], and observe celibacy. (37) They shall not sweep [the house]. (38) They shall not eat meat until the [funeral] offerings are made. (39) On the first, third, fifth, seventh, and ninth days, the water-rite (*udakakriyā*) is performed. (40) And there is the discarding of the clothes. (41) But in the case of the lowest castes, it is at the end [of the period]. (42) From the eruption of the teeth onwards, [the rites] are for both the mother and the father. (43)

There is immediate purification for children, those living in a foreign land, renunciants, and those who are not sapinda relations. [44] And for kings, because of the conflict with their duties. [45] And for a Brahmin, for the sake of not interrupting his Vedic study; for the sake of not interrupting his Vedic study. [46]
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Gautama Dharma Sūtra.

Now, concerning the *śrāddha* (ancestral rite): ||1|| One should offer it to the ancestors on the new moon day. ||2|| Or during the latter fortnight of the month, beginning from the fifth day. ||3|| Or according to one's faith, at any time. ||4|| Or there is no restriction regarding time if suitable materials, a suitable location, and a suitable Brahmin are present. ||5||

One should, according to one's ability, increase the rules regarding the qualities and preparation of the food. (6) One should feed an odd number of guests, with a minimum of nine. (7) Or one may feed them according to one’s enthusiasm. (8) Or one should feed those who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and endowed with eloquence, beauty, youth, and good character. (9) The giving of gifts should first be directed toward the young. (10) Some say that [the young] should be treated like the ancestors (*pitṛ*). (11) And one should not perform the duties of a friend toward them. (12)
In the absence of a son, the sapindas, the mother’s sapindas, and the disciples shall offer [the funeral oblation]. In their absence, the officiating priest and the teacher [shall do so]. (13–14)

By gifts of sesame, mung beans, rice, barley, and water, the ancestors are gratified for one month; by the flesh of fish, deer, ruru antelope, hare, tortoise, boar, and sheep, they are gratified for years; by cow’s milk, milk-rice, and payasa, for twelve years; and by the meat of the vārdhrīṇasa crane, kālaśāka greens, goat, red deer, and rhinoceros—when mixed with honey—the gratification is eternal. (15)

One should not feed a thief, a eunuch, one who has fallen from his caste, an atheist, one who lives as such, one who slays a hero, one who marries before his elder brother, the husband of such a woman, one who lives with his wife’s paramour, a village priest, one who neglects the sacred fires, a drunkard, a rogue, a false witness, a juggler, and those who have abandoned their sacred fires. (16) Nor one whose [younger] brother has married before him; (17) Nor one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa*, a seller of Soma, an arsonist, a poisoner, one who has violated his vow of chastity, a servant of a multitude, one who approaches a woman who should not be approached, a violent man, one who marries before his elder brother, the elder brother so married, one for whom the younger brother has performed the marriage rites, the younger brother who has so performed them, one who abandons his own son, one who has deformed nails, one with black teeth, one with white spots on the skin, the son of a remarried woman, a gambler, one defeated in a wager, a servant of a king, a dealer in substitutes, the husband of a Śūdra woman, one who reviles the Vedas, one afflicted with leprosy, a usurer, a merchant, one who subsists by manual arts, and those whose character is devoted to gambling, instrumental music, clapping, dancing, and singing. (18) Nor those who have been divided against their father's will. (19)
Some [teachers] would feed their disciples and kinsmen; beyond three [such persons], one should feed a person of merit.

One who performs a funeral rite on the same day as death, or one who has sexual intercourse with a Śūdra woman, causes his ancestors to dwell in her excrement for a month. Therefore, on that day, he should observe celibacy.

If one looks upon a dog, a Caṇḍāla, or an outcaste, [the food] becomes defiled. (24) Therefore, one should give [the food] in an enclosed space. (25) Or one should scatter sesame seeds over it. (26) Or a purifier of the row (*paṅktipāvana*) should neutralize the defilement. (27) A purifier of the row is one who knows the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*), a singer of the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*, one who has mastered the three *Nāciketa* fires, one who knows the three *Madhu* verses, one who knows the three *Suparṇa* verses, one who maintains the five sacred fires (*pañcāgni*), a graduate (*snātaka*), one who knows both the Mantra and Brāhmaṇa portions of the Veda, one who knows the Dharma, and one who belongs to a lineage that has received the gift of the Veda from a Brahmin. (28)
And likewise with the sacrificial offerings (havis). ||29|| Some [teachers] say that one should offer dūrvā grass and so forth only at the śrāddha; some say only at the śrāddha. ||30||
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the Gautama Dharmasūtra.

Having performed the Upākarma rite on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, or on the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada, one should study the Vedas for four and a half months, or for five months during the southern course of the sun.
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) who has shaved his hair and body-hair shall not eat meat. Or else, this rule may last for two months.

One should not study when the wind carries dust during the day (5); nor at night when it is audible to the ear (6); nor when there is the sound of arrows, kettledrums, clay drums, or cries of distress (7); nor during the simultaneous howling of dogs, jackals, and donkeys (8); nor when there is redness in the sky, a rainbow, or mist (9); nor when clouds appear outside the rainy season (10); nor when one has urinated or evacuated (11); nor during the night, at the two twilights, or in water (12); nor while it is raining (13); according to some, even when rain-drops fall through the gaps in the roof (14); nor while serving the teacher (15); nor while looking at the heavenly bodies (16); nor when afraid, when riding in a vehicle, when lying down, or with the feet raised (17); nor in a cremation ground, within a village boundary, on a high road, or in a state of impurity (18); nor in the presence of a foul odor, a corpse, a Caṇḍāla, or a Śūdra (19); nor when there is sourness in the mouth or when eructating (20).

The *Ṛgveda*, *Yajurveda*, and the word *Sāman* [are pure] as long as they last. (21) A thunderclap, an earthquake, the appearance of Rāhu, and a meteor are [pure] until the same time [the next day]. (22) Thunder, rain, and lightning [are pure] when fires have been kindled. (23) [This applies] during the day [if it occurs] in the proper season. (24) In the case of lightning, [impurity lasts] through the night, but not beyond the latter part of the night. (25) If [lightning] occurs for more than a third of the night, all [of that night is impure]. (26) According to some, a meteor is the same as lightning. (27) Thunder [is pure] in the afternoon. (28) Even at dusk. (29) The entire night is [pure] until midnight. (30) And if it is daytime, [it is pure] as long as there is light. (31) And when the king residing in one's territory has died. (32) And after returning from a journey together with another person. (33)

One day and night [is the period of impurity] for those who eat at the *śrāddha* of a person who has completed the Veda after a crowded session, or at a human sacrifice (*manuṣyayajña*). (34) Also on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). (35) Or for two days. (36) [The following are also occasions for impurity: the full moon days of Kārttika, Phālguna, and Āṣāḍha. (37)

There are three *aṣṭakā* festivals during the three nights [of the dark fortnights]. According to some, only the last one. [These are observed] on both sides of the rainy season. All [should observe them] when rain, lightning, and thunder occur together. Also when it is raining.

After a meal during a festival; [43] and for one who has completed his Vedic study, for four *muhūrta*s at night; [44] some say this is constant in a city; [45] one is also impure even through mental action; [46] for those performing a *śrāddha*, it lasts until the same time the next day; [47] and likewise when there is contact with one who has performed a *śrāddha* with uncooked food. [48]
And whatever they remember according to each realization, that they remember. ||49||
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Dharmasūtra of Gautama.
A Brāhmaṇa may eat from the hands of twice-born men who are praiseworthy in their own duties; he may also accept gifts from them. 1–2.

Fuel-wood, water, fodder, roots, fruits, honey, *abhayā*, food offered with one's own hands (*abhyudyata*), a bed, a seat, a dwelling, a vehicle, milk, curd, parched grain, fish, *priyaṅgu* rice, meat, paths, and vegetables are not to be refused by anyone from anyone. (3) Furthermore, other things may be accepted for the sake of supporting one's parents, gods, teachers, and dependents. (4) If there is no means of livelihood [for the recipient] other than from a *śūdra*, [the latter may accept such things]. (5) Cattle-herders, cultivators of fields, family friends, those who cause work to be done, and personal attendants—these are persons whose food may be eaten. (6) And a merchant who is not an artisan [is also one whose food may be eaten]. (7)
That which is always unfit to be eaten. ||8||

[Food] contaminated by hair or insects; [food] defiled by the foot of a menstruating woman or a black bird; [food] looked upon by a killer of an embryo; [food] smelled by a cow; [food] corrupted in its internal state; sour gruel that is not curd; food cooked again; stale food—except for vegetables, hard foods, oils, meat, and honey; [food belonging to] those who have abandoned their vows, prostitutes, those accused of crimes, those of unknown origin, staff-bearers (officials), carpenters, misers, prison-keepers, physicians, hunters, those who carry arrows, those who eat the leavings of others, and those who hate the *gaṇas*; [the rule applies] to those excluded from the row of diners prior to Durvāsas; [food] interrupted by eating in vain, by sipping water, or by rising; [food] where the honors are unequal or equal respectively according to whether the guests are of equal or unequal status; and [food] that is unhonored.

The milk of a cow that has not passed ten days since calving during the period of birth-impurity; likewise that of goats and buffaloes [is forbidden during that time]. The milk of sheep is always unfit for drinking, as is that of camels and of animals with uncloven hooves. Also [forbidden is the milk] of those cows that are leaking milk, those that have recently miscarried, and those in heat. And [forbidden is the milk] of a cow whose calf is dead.

Among five-toed animals, the porcupine, hare, porcupine-squirrel, iguana, rhinoceros, and tortoise are edible. (27) Those with teeth in both jaws, those with hair on their bodies, those that are hairless, those with solid hooves, the sparrow, the water-fowl, the ruddy goose, and the swan are not to be eaten. (28) The crow, the heron, the vulture, the hawk, water-birds, those with red feet or red beaks, the domestic cock, and the domestic pig are not to be eaten. (29) Nor are the cow and the ox. (30) Meat that is not offered [to gods or ancestors], meat from a dying animal, and meat not intended for sacrifice are forbidden. (31) Sprouts, garlic, onions, and exudations are forbidden. (32) Red juices and the products of incision are forbidden. (33) The *nicud*, woodpecker, crane, *balāka* crane, parrot, cormorant, *ṭiṭṭibha* bird, *māndhāla*, and nocturnal prowlers are not to be eaten. (34)

Those that peck with their beaks, those that scratch with their claws, and web-footed birds may be eaten. (35) Fish may also be eaten, provided they are not prepared as a delicacy. (36) Animals may be killed for the sake of dharma. (37) One should consume meat from animals killed by predators, or meat whose defects have not been seen, after sprinkling it with water and having it praised with words; one should consume it. (38)
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the Gautama Dharmasūtra.
A woman has no independence in religious matters (dharma). (1) She should not transgress against her husband. (2) She should be restrained in speech, sight, and action. (3)

One who has no husband and desires offspring may obtain [a son] from her brother-in-law (devarāt). ||4|| A woman authorized by her teacher (guru) shall not let the fertile season pass by. ||5|| [She may obtain offspring] from those related by funeral offerings (piṇḍa), by lineage (gotra), or by ṛṣis, or even from one related only by birth (yonimātra). ||6|| Some say she must not [obtain offspring] from her brother-in-law. ||7|| She shall not do so for more than once. ||8||

The offspring belongs to the progenitor. ||9|| Except by agreement. ||10|| And [the offspring] belongs to the owner of the field while he is alive. ||11|| If [the seed was] from another, it belongs to him. ||12|| Or it belongs to both. ||13|| But because of protection, it belongs to the husband alone. ||14||

If the husband has disappeared, she shall wait for six years; if he is heard of, she may go to him. But if he has entered a religious order, there is a cessation of her duty [to him], because of the risk of attachment. In the case of a Brahmin, the period is twelve years when the separation is due to his pursuit of learning.
In the same manner, when the elder brother is present, the younger brother may marry a maiden or establish the sacred fires; however, some say he must wait for six years.

Having passed three menstrual periods, a maiden should choose a husband for herself, discarding her paternal ornaments, provided she is blameless. (20) The giving [of the girl] takes place before the onset of menstruation. (21) He who does not give her away is at fault. (22) Some say that the time for giving is before she has put on the marriage garment. (23)

One may take property from a Śūdra for the purpose of accomplishing a marriage, or when there is a connection with the performance of religious duties; (24) likewise from a Śūdra who possesses many cattle but performs low deeds; (25) from one who owns a hundred cows but has not maintained the sacred fires; (26) and from one who owns a thousand cows but does not drink the Soma juice. (27)
And having not enjoyed the seventh [day's] food, one may store for the sake of accumulation; even from those who have not diminished their ritual duties.

If questioned by the king, he should speak [the truth]. (30) For if he is endowed with learning and good character, he must be supported by him. (31) If there is an obstruction to the system of dharma, it is a fault if he fails to act. (32) It is a fault. (32)
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the Gāutama-dharmasūtra.
The duty of the social classes and the duty of the stages of life have been explained. ||1||

Now, indeed, this person is tainted by a blameworthy act, such as officiating at a sacrifice for which one should not officiate, eating what is unfit to be eaten, speaking what is censurable, failing to perform what is prescribed for the learned, and practicing what is forbidden. Regarding this, they deliberate: "Should he perform an expiation, or should he not?"

"One should not perform [the sacrifice]," so they say; "for indeed, karma is not exhausted. "One should perform it," says another. It is known from scripture: "Having sacrificed with the *punaḥstoma*, they return to the Soma-pressing. And: "And having sacrificed with the *vrātyastomas*. And: "He who sacrifices with the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) overcomes all evil, he overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin. And: "One should cause him who is being falsely accused to sacrifice with the *agniṣṭut*."

The means of expiation for that [sin] are: recitation (*japa*), austerity (*tapas*), burnt offerings (*homa*), fasting (*upavāsa*), and giving gifts (*dāna*). (11) The Upaniṣads, the Vedāntas, the *Saṃhitās* among all the meters, the *Madhu* hymns, the *Aghamarṣaṇa*, the *Atharvaśiras*, the *Rudras*, the *Puruṣasūkta*, the *Rājan* and *Rauhiṇa* Sāmans, the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara*, the *Puruṣagati*, the *Mahānāmnīs*, the *Mahāvairāja*, the *Mahādivākīrtya*, any one of the *Jyeṣṭhasāmans*, the *Bahiṣpavamāna*, the *Kūṣmāṇḍas*, the *Pāvamānīs*, and the *Sāvitrī*—these are the purifiers (*pāvana*). (12) The practice of a milk-vow, subsisting on vegetables, subsisting on fruits, barley-gruel in a handful (*prasṛti*), the consumption of gold, the consumption of clarified butter, and the drinking of *soma*—these are the means of purification (*medhya*). (13) All mountains, all rivers, sacred lakes, holy fords (*tīrtha*), the dwellings of seers (*ṛṣi*), cow-pens, and crossroads—these are the [sanctified] places. (14) Celibacy (*brahmacarya*), speaking the truth, touching water at the [three] pressings of the day, wearing wet clothes, sleeping on the ground, and fasting—these are the austerities (*tapas*). (15) Gold, a cow, clothing, a horse, land, sesame seeds, clarified butter, and food—these are the things to be given. (16) One year, six months, four, three, two, or one [month]; twenty-four days, twelve days, six days, three days, or a day and night—these are the durations of time. (17)

These very [penances] shall be performed optionally when no specific instruction is given. (18) For heavy sins, the penances are heavy; for light sins, they are light. (19) The Kṛcchra, the Atikṛcchra, and the Cāndrāyaṇa constitute the universal expiation—the universal expiation. (20)
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the Gautamīya Dharmasūtra.

One should abandon a father who is a regicide, a priest for Śūdras, a priest for the sake of a Śūdra, a corrupter of the Vedas, a killer of an embryo, or one who lives with outcastes (antāvasāyin) or with a woman of the outcaste class. (1) Having assembled his teachers of knowledge and his blood relations, they shall perform for him all the funeral rites, beginning with the water libations. (2) They shall overturn his sacrificial vessel. (3) A slave or a laborer, having brought a vessel from the refuse heap and filled it with impure water from a jar belonging to a female slave, shall, facing south, overturn it with his foot while pronouncing the name [of the deceased], saying: "I deprive so-and-so of water. (4) All [the relatives] shall touch him [the corpse or the vessel], wearing their sacred threads over the right shoulder and with their hair-locks loosened. (5) The teachers of knowledge and the blood relations shall look upon [the vessel]. (6) Having touched water, they enter the village. (7)
After that, having conversed with him, he should remain for one night reciting the Sāvitrī if [the conversation occurred] through ignorance; but if it was intentional, for three nights.

But he who is purified by penance—once he is purified—they should fill a vessel made of gold with water from a most holy pool or from flowing rivers and have him touch that water. (10) Then they should give that vessel to him; having accepted it, he should recite: "Peaceful is heaven, peaceful is earth, peaceful and auspicious is the intermediate space; I take hold here of that which is luminous. (11) With these Yajus formulas, with the Pāvamānī verses, with the Taratsamandī verses, and with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras, he should offer oblations of clarified butter. (12) He should give gold or a cow to a Brāhmaṇa. (13) And also to his teacher. (14)
But he for whom the penance ends with death shall be purified upon dying. They should perform for him all the funeral rites, beginning with the water libations.
This very same water for pacification [is prescribed] for all minor offenses (upapātaka). ||17||
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the Gautama Dharmasūtra.

1. A slayer of a Brāhmaṇa, a drinker of spirituous liquor, one who violates the bed of his guru, one who has sexual intercourse with women related by birth or marriage to his mother or father, a thief, an atheist, one who habitually performs censurable acts, one who abandons those who must not be abandoned, and one who abandons those who are fallen—these are the fallen (patita). 2. And those who associate with such persons [are also fallen]. 3. By associating with them for one year, one becomes fallen as well.
Falling away from the duties of the twice-born is degradation (patana). And there is failure to attain [the goal] in the next world. Some consider that [degradation] itself to be hell.
The first three [offenses] are inexpressible, according to Manu. Some say that one does not fall [from the status of a monk] by violating the precept regarding those who are not one's guru’s wives.
A woman falls [from her caste] by causing a miscarriage or by serving a man of a lower varṇa. 9.
Giving false testimony, slandering the king, and making a false accusation against one's teacher are equal to mortal sins (pātaka). ||10||

Among those unworthy of sitting in the same row as the twice-born, up to the point before Durvāla, the minor offenses (upapātaka) consist of killing a cow, slaying a Brahmin, composing heterodox mantras, violating a vow of chastity, and having lost the right to recite the Sāvitrī.

The officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and the teacher (*ācārya*) are to be abandoned for teaching what is unknown and for serving those who have fallen from their status. (12) One falls [from his own status] by abandoning them in any other case. (13) And some say that the one who accepts gifts from such a person also falls. (14)
There shall never be a lack of maintenance for the mother and father. However, they shall not divide the inheritance.

The guilt is equal [to that of killing a Brahmin] in the case of falsely accusing a Brahmin (17). It is double [the guilt] in the case of one who is innocent (18). And likewise in the case of harming a weak person when one is capable of rescuing him (19). For threatening a Brahmin while enraged, there is no heaven for a hundred years (20). For striking him, a thousand years (21). Upon seeing blood, he shall collect as many particles of dust as are scattered by it; he shall collect them again and again (22).
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the Gautama Dharmasūtra.
Expiation. ||1||

The killer of a Brahmin may cast himself three times into a fire of chopped wood. Or he may become a target for those bearing weapons in a battle. Or, carrying a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) and a skull-bowl in his hands, observing celibacy for twelve years, he may enter a village for alms, proclaiming his deed. He should step aside from the path upon seeing an Ārya. By alternating between standing and sitting and bathing in water at the three daily libations, he shall be purified. Or, if he risks his life for the sake of a Brahmin, he is purified. Or, if he has successfully repelled an attack three times or more, he is purified. Or, at the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), he is purified. This applies even at another sacrifice, provided it concludes with the *agniṣṭut* rite.

If [the offense] has been committed, [the penance applies] even without having killed in the case of killing a Brāhmaṇa; ||11|| and likewise in the case of an Ātreyī woman; ||12|| and also in the case of an embryo of a Brāhmaṇa that was not known [to be such]. ||13||

For killing a Kṣatriya, one shall observe the standard vow of celibacy for six years and give a thousand cows with a bull as the eleventh. For a Vaiśya, one shall observe it for three years and give a hundred cows with a bull as the eleventh. For a Śūdra, one shall observe it for one year and give eleven cows with a bull as the eleventh. The same applies for killing an Ātreyī woman.

And for killing a cow, as in the case of a Vaiśya; [18] and also for the killing of frogs, mongooses, crows, *bimba* birds, porcupines, mice, and dogs; [19] having killed a thousand vertebrate animals; [20] and for the killing of boneless animals or a load of oxen; [21] or alternatively, one should give some small gift for each individual vertebrate animal killed. [22]

For a eunuch, a load of straw and a māṣa of lead; ||23|| for a boar, a jar of ghee; ||24|| for a snake, an iron staff; ||25|| for a loose woman who is a nominal Brahmin wife, a *jīla* [fine]; ||26|| in the case of a prostitute, nothing at all. ||27||

For the loss of a bed, food, or wealth, there shall be one year’s penance for each; [for killing] a Brahmin, twelve years. (28) In the case of adultery with another's wife, two years. (29) In the case of a learned Śrotriya, three years. (30) And in the case of obtaining property through forbidden means, there shall be renunciation [of that property]. (31) Or he may restore it to its proper place. (32) If one employs forbidden mantras, [the penance lasts] for a thousand recitations of the Veda. (33) The same applies to those who extinguish the sacred fires, those who neglect their studies, and those who commit minor offenses (upapātaka). (34) A woman who has committed adultery, even if she is protected, shall nevertheless receive her maintenance. (35)
For intercourse with non-human females—with the exception of cows—on account of a woman, there shall be an oblation of ghee with the *kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras; [an oblation of ghee]. ||36||
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the Gautama Dharmasūtra.

They should pour hot liquor into the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk liquor; when he is dead, he shall be purified. (1) If one drinks it unintentionally, he must consume hot milk, ghee, water, or air for three days each; this is the Kṛcchra penance, after which his consecration (funeral rites) may take place. (2) The same applies to swallowing urine, feces, or semen. (3) And to consuming the flesh of carnivorous beasts, camels, or donkeys. (4) And to the flesh of domestic cocks or pigs. (5) For smelling the odor of liquor, there shall be breath-suppressions (prāṇāyāmas) and the consumption of ghee. (6) The same applies to one bitten by the aforementioned creatures. (7)

One who has violated the Guru’s bed shall lie upon a heated iron bed (8). Or he shall embrace a glowing metal image (sūrmi) (9). Or, having had his penis and testicles cut off and holding them in his cupped hands, he shall walk straight toward the southwest until his body collapses (10). When dead, he shall be purified (11).

[Sexual intercourse] with a female friend, a woman born of the same womb, a woman of the same lineage, the wife of a pupil, a daughter-in-law, or a cow is equal to [the sin of violating] one's own bed (talpasama). Some say it is equivalent to [the sin of] throwing refuse.
