If a woman has intercourse with a man of lower caste, the king shall have her devoured by dogs in public; he shall cause the man to be executed, or as previously prescribed.

One who has spilled his semen should sacrifice to Nirṛti at a crossroads using a donkey. Having put on its hide with the hair turned upward and carrying a red vessel, he should go about begging for alms from seven houses, proclaiming his deed. After one year, he becomes pure. In the event of the emission of semen caused by fear or disease, or during an emission in a dream, there shall be an offering of clarified butter into the fire for seven nights, or an oblation of two fuel-sticks with the two *retasyā* verses, provided that the kindling of the fire and the practice of begging have not been performed.

A student who has risen with the sun shall remain standing for the day without eating, and one who has seen the sun set shall remain sitting for the night, reciting the Sāvitrī. Having seen something impure, he should look at the sun after performing breath control (prāṇāyāma).

In the case of eating what should not be eaten, one becomes free of excrement [by fasting]. (23) Fasting for at least three nights [is required]. (24) Or, consuming fruits that have fallen of their own accord for seven nights, provided one does not exceed [the permitted quantity]. (25) For eating [forbidden food] prior to the five-clawed animals, there is emesis and the consumption of clarified butter. (26)

For verbal abuse, falsehood, and violence, the penance lasts for three nights at most. (27) For speaking untruth, there should be an oblation with the Vāruṇī and Mānavī verses. (28) Some maintain that there is no fault in falsehood when it concerns marriage, sexual intercourse, jesting, or a situation involving distress. (29)

But indeed, one must not lie for the sake of a teacher. One who speaks a falsehood to a teacher, even regarding a trivial matter, kills seven generations of men—both preceding and succeeding him—even if he does so only in his mind.

For approaching an outcaste woman (antāvasāyinī), there is a year-long kṛcchra penance. (32) If it was unintentional, it is for twelve nights. (33) For approaching a woman in her courses (udakyā), it is three nights; [this is repeated] three nights. (34)
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the Gautama Dharma Sūtra.

The secret expiation for a fault that has not been made public is as follows: 1. One who desires to accept what should not be accepted, or who has already accepted it, should recite over water the four verses beginning with "taratsamandī. 2. One who desires to eat what is unfit to be eaten should scatter [grain] over the earth.
Some [hold that] there is purification from sexual intercourse during the other seasons by touching water; others [hold this applies] regarding women [in general]. 4–5.

Or, one may observe the vow of milk for ten nights, the second with ghee, and the third with water; eating only once during the day, wearing clothes moistened with water, one performs the oblation of hair, nails, skin, flesh, blood, sinews, bone, and marrow, ending with: "I offer myself into the mouth of Death. This is the expiation for all [sins], including the killing of a learned Brahmin (*bhrūṇahatyā*). Now, another [method]. The rule has been stated. One should offer oblations with the *mahāvyāhṛtis* and with the *kūṣmāṇḍa* verses, using clarified butter.

Or, observing that very same vow, one who is exhausted by breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) for the [sins of] killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, or violating the Guru’s bed should mutter the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn; this is equal to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice.
Or, by repeating the Sāvitrī one thousand times, he indeed purifies himself. Or, by repeating the Aghamarṣaṇa three times while submerged in water, he is released from all sins; he is released.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the Gautama Dharmasūtra.

Regarding this, they ask: "In how many ways does one who has broken his vow of chastity (avakīrṇin) enter [the gods]? [The answer is: "Into the Maruts by means of his breath, into Indra by means of his strength, into Bṛhaspati by means of his spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa), and into Agni by means of all the rest. On the night of the new moon, having kindled the fire, he offers two expiatory oblations of clarified butter: "I am one who has spilled his seed through desire; I am one who has spilled his seed, O Desire! To Desire, Svāhā! and "I am one who has been deceived by desire; I have been deceived, O Desire! To Desire, Svāhā! Having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, sprinkled water around it, and performed the ritual act of establishing the sacrificial site, he stands up and worships the fire three times with the verse: "May they sprinkle me... "This is for the conquest of these worlds, for the mastery of these worlds," so it is said. According to some, this rite applies specifically to one who might be as if unpurified; such a person should offer the oblation in this manner and recite the mantra in this manner. A choice gift (vara) is the sacrificial fee, since no specific rule is given regarding the expiation.

Having discharged semen in a Śūdra woman, in a non-vaginal opening, or in connection with a blameworthy act—even if done intentionally—after engaging in crookedness, calumny, forbidden conduct, or eating forbidden food, one should touch water while reciting verses addressed to the waters (*abliṅga*), verses addressed to Varuṇa (*vāruṇī*), or other purificatory texts. For transgressions of speech or mind involving forbidden things, the five *vyāhṛtis* are prescribed.

In all cases, one should sip water with the formula: "May the day and the sun purify me," in the morning; and "May the night and Varuṇa [purify me]," in the evening. Or, one should offer eight fuel-sticks with the verse beginning "devakṛtasya" (RV X.164.3); by merely offering them, one is released from every sin—yes, one is released.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the Gautama Dharmasūtra.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the Kṛcchra penances. (1) Having eaten sacrificial food for breakfast, one should not eat for three nights. (2) Then, for another three days, one should eat only at night. (3) Then, for another three days, one should not beg for anything. (4) Then, for another three days, one should fast. (5)

One who desires speed should stand during the day and sit during the night. (6) One should speak the truth. (7) One should not converse with those who are ignoble. (8) One should constantly recite the *raurava* and *yaudhājaya* [Sāmans]. (9) At each of the three daily libations (*anusavana*), one should touch water and purify oneself with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," which contain the word *pavitra*, and with the eight verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ. (10)
Now follows the libation of water (udakatarpaṇa). ||11||

Homage to Ahamāya, Mohamāya, Maṃhamāya, to the Shaker (Dhūnvate), to the Ascetic (Tāpasa), to Punarvasu; homage! Homage to Mauñjyāya, to Ūrmyāya, to Vasuvinda, to Sarvavinda; homage! Homage to Pāra, to Supāra, to Mahāpāra, to the One who causes one to cross over; homage! Homage to Rudra, to Paśupati, to the Great God, to Tryambaka, to the Solitary Wanderer, to the Overlord, to Hara, to Śarva, to Īśāna, to Ugra, to the Wielder of the Thunderbolt, to the Compassionate One, to the One with Matted Hair; homage! Homage to Sūrya, to Āditya; homage! Homage to the Blue-necked One, to the White-throated One; homage! Homage to the Black One, to the Tawny One; homage! Homage to the Eldest, to the Best, to the Ancient, to Indra, to the Golden-haired One, to the One whose Vital Energy is Upward-turned; homage! Homage to the True, to the Purifier, to the One of Purifying Color, to Desire, to the One who takes any form at will; homage! Homage to the Radiant, to the One of Radiant Form; homage! Homage to the Sharp, to the One of Sharp Form; homage! Homage to the Auspicious One, to the Excellent Man, to the Great Man, to the Middle Man, to the Supreme Man, to the Vow-observer; homage! Homage to the Moon-browed One, to the One clad in a Skin; homage! Thus [ends the section]. 12.

This indeed is the worship of the Sun (13). These indeed are the oblations of clarified butter (14). At the end of the twelve nights, having cooked a sacrificial porridge (*caru*), one should offer it to these deities (15): "To Agni, Svāhā! To Soma, Svāhā! To Agni and Soma, to Indra and Agni, to Indra, to the Viśvedevas, to Brahmā, to Prajāpati, and to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, [Svāhā]! (16). Then follows the gratification of the Brāhmaṇas (17).
By this very [rule], the *atikṛcchra* is explained. (18) He should eat only as much as he would take up [in his hand] once. (19)
Subsisting on water is the third; that is the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. ||20||

Having performed it once, he becomes pure, cleansed, and fit for ritual action. Having performed it a second time, he is liberated from whatever sin he commits other than the great mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*). Having performed it a third time, he removes all transgression.
Now, having performed these three *kṛcchra* penances, one becomes bathed in all the Vedas; one becomes known by all the gods—both he who knows this, and he who knows this. ||24–25||
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the Gautama Dharmasūtra.

Now, therefore, follows the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Its procedure has been explained in connection with the Kṛcchra. There is shaving of the head and the observance of vows. On the day after the full moon, he should fast. With the verses "Āpyāyasva," "Saṃ te payāṃsi," and "Navo nava," he should perform the libation of water, the oblation of clarified butter, the consecration of the sacrificial food, and the worship of the moon. He should offer oblations with the four verses beginning "Yad devā devaheḍanam. At the end, he should offer fuel-sticks with the verse "Devakṛtasya."

With the formulas “Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ,” “tapaḥ,” “satyam,” “yaśaḥ,” “śrīḥ,” “ūrk,” “iḍā,” “ojas,” “tejaḥ,” “puruṣaḥ,” “dharmaḥ,” and “śivaḥ,” he should mentally consecrate each morsel with its respective mantra. Or, he may consecrate all of them together with “namas” and “svāhā. The size of a morsel is that which does not distort the mouth.
Caru, alms-food, barley-meal, grain-particles, barley-gruel, vegetables, milk, curd, ghee, roots, fruits, and water—these sacrificial offerings are increasingly praised in the sequence listed. ||11||

On the full moon day, having eaten fifteen mouthfuls, one should eat during the latter fortnight by decreasing the amount by one each day. (12) Having fasted on the new moon day, one should eat during the former fortnight by increasing the amount by one each day. (13) According to some, this is the reverse. (14) This is the Cāndrāyaṇa month. (15)

Having attained this, one who is free from evil and free from sin destroys all transgression. (16) Having attained the second [stage], he purifies ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself as the twenty-first, as well as the lineage. (17) And having attained the year-long [fast], he attains the same world as the moon; he attains it. (18)
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the Gautama Dharmasūtra.

After the father's death, the sons shall divide the inheritance. (1) Or, while the mother is still living, they may divide it after her menses have ceased and with her consent. (2) Alternatively, the eldest son may take the entire estate and support the others like a father. (3) However, in the case of partition, there is an increase in spiritual merit. (4)

A twentieth part for the eldest: a pair of animals, a chariot yoked on both sides, and a bull. (5) For the middle son: one-eyed, lame, hornless, or tailless animals, provided there are many of them. (6) A sheep, an iron vessel, a house with its furniture, and one each of four-footed animals for the youngest. (7) Everything else shall be divided equally. (8)

Or the first-born may take two shares. (9) Each of the others may take one share. (10) Or, each desirable item of property, the elder brother shall receive one by one. (11) [This applies to] ten of each kind of livestock. (12) Not so for single-hoofed animals or bipeds. (13) A bull is the additional share for the eldest. (14) A bull as the sixteenth is the additional share for the son of the eldest wife. (15) The younger brothers shall share equally with the son of the eldest wife. (16)
Or there may be a specific division of shares according to each mother within one's own group. ||17||

A man who has no son should give away a daughter as an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), having offered oblations to Agni and Prajāpati and having made an agreement that "this offspring shall be for us. According to some, she becomes an appointed daughter by the mere intention [of the father]. Because of the uncertainty regarding that [status], one should not marry a girl who has no brother.
Those related by funeral offerings, lineage, or ancestral sages shall divide the inheritance; and a woman shall share it if he leaves no offspring. 21.
Or one should seek seed [from another]. (22) In Devaravatī, that which is born from another is without a share. (23)

A woman’s property belongs to her daughters who are unmarried and not established [in life]. (24) The dowry of a sister belongs to the uterine brothers after the death of the mother. (25) And some say it belongs to them even before [the mother's death]. (26)

The division of the inheritance among those who were not reunited belongs to the eldest son of the deceased. (27) When one who was reunited dies, the one who was reunited is the heir to his property. (28) A son born after partition inherits only from the father. (29)
A physician should not, at his own will, give what he has earned himself to those who are unlearned [in medicine]. (30) Those who are unlearned should divide it equally. (31)

The sons born of the body (*aurasa*), the son of the wife (*kṣetraja*), the adopted son (*dattaka*), the son made (*kṛtrima*), the son secretly born (*gūḍhotpanna*), and the cast-off son (*apaviddha*) are the heirs to the estate (*rikthabhāj*). ||32|| The son born of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*), the son of a pregnant bride (*sahoḍha*), the son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*), the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*), the son given himself (*svayaṃdatta*), and the bought son (*krīta*) are the sharers of the family name (*gotrabhāj*). ||33|| In the absence of the sons beginning with the *aurasa*, they are entitled to one-fourth of a share (*caturthāṃśin*). ||34||

The eldest son of a Brāhmaṇa by a Kṣatriya wife, if endowed with good qualities, shares equally [in the inheritance]. (35) The other [sons] receive their shares minus the portion due to the eldest. (36) In the case of a combination of sons born of a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya wife, they share in the same manner as with the son of the Brāhmaṇa wife. (37) This applies even if the father was a Kṣatriya. (38) Even the son of a Śūdra wife, if he is obedient and there are no other offspring, shall receive the means for his livelihood according to the rule for a pupil. (39)
According to some, even the son of a wife of the same caste does not receive [the inheritance] if he has behaved improperly.
The Vedic scholars shall divide the inheritance of a childless Brāhmaṇa; for others, the king [shall take it].

The dull-witted and the impotent are to be maintained [by the family]. ||43|| The offspring of one who is dull-witted is entitled to a share. ||44|| As in the case of the son of a Śūdra woman, so it is with those born of women in the inverse order of castes (pratiloma). ||45||
There is no sharing of food prepared for the sake of water and security; nor is there sharing with women who are married to others. 46–47.

When a matter is not already known, that which is praised by at least ten learned men—those who possess the *ūha* [analytical knowledge], are free from greed, and are upright—should be performed. (48) Four who have mastered the four Vedas, three who belong to the stages of life (*āśrama*) prior to the last one, and three who individually know the Dharma; these ten at minimum are called an assembly (*pariṣad*). (49) In the absence of these, however, a learned man (*śrotriya*) who knows the Veda and is upright shall decide in case of disagreement. (50) For he is incapable of inflicting harm or bestowing favor upon living beings. (51)
Through the specific practice of the dharmas, one who knows the dharma attains the heavenly world by means of both knowledge and resolute application. ||52||
Thus, dharma is dharma. ||53||
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the Gautama Dharmasūtra.
And thus the Gautamiya Dharmasūtra is completed.
